word_families_grade1.reading:
## Learn One, Read Many

Read this **word**: cat. Look at each **letter**. Say the sounds with help. Put the **sounds** together.

Now read hat, bat, mat, sat, rat and pat. The ending **chunk** at stays the same. The **start** changes. This word **family** has the same ending letters and sounds.

Try hop, mop, top and pop. What stays the same? The ending is op. This shared ending is a **pattern**.

Try stop. The s and t make a **blend**. You can hear both sounds. In shop, sh makes one sound. In chop, ch makes one sound too. A pair like sh is called a digraph. Shop, chop and stop all end in op.

Cat and hat **rhyme**. Their sounds match from the a to the end. A **vowel** letter can help spell this part. A, e, i, o and u are vowel letters. Y can do this job too.

Rhymes need not have the same spelling. Some and hum rhyme in the way we say them here. People may say words in different ways.

Check the whole word. A picture can show what it means. It cannot tell you how to read each letter. Ask for a model or help that works for you.

glossary.Word: Something we say, sign or write that has meaning.
glossary.Letter: A mark in the alphabet, such as a or b.
glossary.Sound: A part we hear in speech, such as /m/ in mat.
glossary.Chunk: Here, the ending part, such as at in cat.
glossary.Start: The first part of a word.
glossary.Family: Here, words with the same ending letters and sounds.
glossary.Rhyme: To sound the same from the vowel to the end, like cat and hat.
glossary.Vowel: A, e, i, o, u, and sometimes y. These letters can spell the sounds in the middle of cat and sit.
glossary.Blend: Two or more consonant sounds side by side. You hear each one, as in st in stop.
glossary.Pattern: A part that repeats, such as at in cat and hat.

faq: Some words have a part that does not fit the pattern you know. Look at that part with your teacher. Then read the whole word.
There are many. Learn a few at a time. Read each whole word too.
Words in these spelling families rhyme. But some and hum rhyme here even though their endings look different.
Ask for help that works for you. Your teacher can show a model and help you compare the written endings too.
Yes. Long words have parts too. Your teacher can help you find parts you know.
Yes. Sh in shop makes one sound. St in stop is different: you hear /s/ and /t/.

story_retell_grade2.reading:
## Retell a Story in Three Parts

A **story** tells about people, animals or other **characters** and what they do. To **retell**, tell the key events in your own words.

The **beginning** often tells who is there. It may show the **setting**: where and when the story takes place. In the **middle**, more things happen. A **problem** may lead someone to try a new plan. The **end** shows how the story finishes. Some stories have a **solution**. Others leave a question open.

Here is a made-up story. Ada gets a puppy. It chews her shoe, hat and library book. She hides her things. The puppy finds them. Then Ada gives it a rope toy. It chews the toy, and her shoes are safe.

First, the puppy arrives. Next, it chews things. Ada's first plan does not work. At the end, the toy helps. This is a story, not advice on how to train a real puppy.

Keep the events in **order** so others can follow them. You may speak, write, point to pictures or use your talk device. Check the story if you forget.

The word but can show a change: Ada liked her puppy, but it chewed her things. Look at what happens. A story need not use but to show a problem.

glossary.Story: A telling of events that are real or made up.
glossary.Beginning: The first part. It often shows who is there and where they are.
glossary.Middle: The part between the start and the end, where events unfold.
glossary.End: The last part. A problem may be solved or left open.
glossary.Character: A person, animal or other being in a story.
glossary.Solution: A way to deal with or solve a problem.
glossary.Retell: Tell the key events again in your own words. Keep their meaning.

faq: Some stories have more than one. Tell the events that matter most. Show how they connect.
Reading aloud uses the words on the page. A retell uses your own words. You can also use pictures or a talk device.
Tell enough for someone to follow the key events. Ask what part they want you to explain.
Go back to the story. Look at the pictures. What happened after the start and before the end?
You can use a start, middle and end to tell about your day. A true story need not have a problem.
Some stories do that. In this task, tell the events from first to last so your listener can follow them.
memory: Put three cards in a row: beginning, middle, end. Point to each as you tell the puppy story. Use words, pictures or your talk device.
The cards help you keep the events in order. Choose a way to use them that works for you.
Ada liked her puppy, but it chewed her things. But shows a change here. Draw a door to help you think of a change.
The door is a memory cue. Not every story uses but. Check what happens in the story.

figurative_language_grade5.reading:
## The Sideways Sentence

On the first day of school, Marisol's stomach was a washing machine on spin cycle.

This made-up sentence is a **metaphor**. Her stomach is not a machine. The words suggest a churning, nervous feeling. **Figurative language** uses words beyond their **literal**, or plain, meaning. It can help us share an idea, but a reader may need help to understand it.

A **simile** uses like or as to **compare** unlike things: “The hallway was as loud as a stadium.” Both places are noisy. “I like apples” is not a simile. It does not compare two things.

A metaphor can say, “The hallway was a stadium.” It links the noise and bustle of the two places. A metaphor need not use the word is. Neither kind of comparison is always better. Choose what fits your meaning.

**Personification** gives human traits to something that is not human. “The alarm clock scolded me” gives the clock a human purpose. A clock can make noise, but it cannot choose to scold you.

**Hyperbole** stretches the truth for effect: “This school backpack weighs a thousand pounds!” The speaker means it feels very heavy. The speaker is not trying to fool us. A reader needs context to spot the stretch. An unclear joke can still mislead.

An **idiom** is a phrase with a shared meaning you may not get from each word. Marisol tells a joke to “break the ice.” She helps people feel at ease; she does not smash ice. Check the scene or a dictionary. Ask a speaker if the phrase is new to you. Idioms can differ across languages and groups.

These tools can overlap. An idiom may also be a metaphor. In our sort, choose the main tool the sentence shows. Explain what it means.

**Imagery** appeals to our senses. “The warm bread smelled sweet” may be literal and still create an image. A **symbol** stands for a larger idea in a story. A key might stand for belonging, if the story supports that view. It need not mean that in every story.

Try a vivid version and a plain version of one thought. Ask a reader what each means. Choose words that help your reader. Keep facts such as dates and places clear.

glossary.Simile: A comparison of unlike things using like or as.
glossary.Metaphor: A way to describe one thing as another, without a like or as comparison.
glossary.Personification: Giving human traits or feelings to something that is not human.
glossary.Hyperbole: A statement that stretches the truth for effect.
glossary.Idiom: A phrase with a shared meaning you may not get from its words alone.
glossary.Literal: Using the plain meaning of words in that setting.
glossary.Figurative: Using words beyond their plain meaning, such as a comparison.
glossary.Imagery: Words that appeal to sight, sound, touch, taste or smell.
glossary.Compare: Look at how things are alike or different.
glossary.Symbol: Something that stands for a larger idea in a story or setting.

faq: It means it is raining very hard. This lesson does not tell us how the phrase began. Do not guess its history and call the guess a fact.
Yes. People use it to wish a performer good luck. That tells us its meaning, but not exactly how it began.
A reader needs to see the link. An unusual comparison can work if the writer makes that link clear.
Some have similar phrases. Others do not. Ask a speaker or check a dictionary. A word-for-word translation may not make sense.
A lie aims to fool someone. Hyperbole asks the reader to spot a stretch. Still, an unclear stretch can fool a reader, so think about who will read it.
It gives you more ways to share meaning. Plain words matter too. Try both and ask which best fits your purpose.

argument_evidence_grade6.reading:
## Says Who?

“We should keep the library open until five.” This is a **claim**: a statement the writer wants us to accept. It calls for an action. A claim can also be about a **fact**, such as the library's closing time. Facts and claims are not opposites.

An **argument** gives support for a claim. **Evidence** is information used as support. It can be a record, an observation, an example or an exact quote. **Reasoning** explains how the evidence supports the claim. It also shows the limits of that link.

Try this made-up case. A school has 120 students in one year group. In a week, a librarian records 40 different students using the library after three. These are invented numbers for practice, not research results.

A writer wants later opening hours. Forty is one third of 120. The record shows that some students use the library after school. It does not show that all 40 want to stay until five. It also says nothing about staffing costs. The writer needs more evidence for those points.

Here is another made-up case. Six of eleven team members have a fixed plan on Tuesdays. That supports a claim that Tuesday practice is hard for many to attend. It does not show that Thursday is better. Check their plans for Thursday too. Reasoning cannot take the place of missing evidence.

A **counterclaim** is an opposing claim. A person may also question the evidence or the link between it and the claim. Give a fair account of a strong objection. A **rebuttal** responds with reasons and evidence. It may admit a limit or lead the writer to change the claim.

A fact is something that is the case. A statement that claims to be a fact still needs checking. An **opinion** is a belief, judgment or preference. An opinion about school policy can have good reasons behind it. Calling it an opinion does not settle the debate.

Evidence is **relevant** when it bears on the exact claim. The wall color will not settle how late the library should stay open. Check the **source**, how the information was gathered, and what else might explain it. Check arguments you agree with too.

In the sort, read each statement's role in its made-up case. A statement can serve as evidence even though someone is also claiming it is true. Use the words as well as the picture.

glossary.Claim: A statement someone wants others to accept. It can be about a fact, a value or an action.
glossary.Evidence: Information used to support a claim. Check whether it is sound and fits the question.
glossary.Reasoning: An explanation of how evidence supports a claim and where that link has limits.
glossary.Counterclaim: A claim that opposes another claim.
glossary.Fact: Something that is the case. Check the evidence for a statement that claims to be a fact.
glossary.Opinion: A belief, judgment or preference. It may have reasons behind it.
glossary.Relevant: Related to the exact claim or question being discussed.
glossary.Source: Where information comes from, such as a person, text or record.
glossary.Rebuttal: A response to an opposing claim or objection, backed by reasons.

faq: An opinion can be a belief, judgment or preference. It can have good reasons behind it. A claim may be about a fact or an action, so facts and claims are not opposites.
Yes. A true detail may not help answer the question. First check that it is true. Then ask how it supports this claim.
No. Check the quality and fit of the evidence. A pile of weak examples may still leave a gap.
Look for a serious objection or another way to explain the evidence. Do not invent an equal case for both sides when the evidence does not support that.
A class task may ask you to study a view you do not hold. Explain it fairly. Make clear that it is an exercise, and do not make up support.
Yes. People of any age can miss a weak link. Check the specific argument and its evidence.

brief.context:
Classroom practice: one grant can fund one of four plans. All records below are made up. Judge the arguments as written. A real decision would need checked costs and more facts.
A. Library: Try keeping it open until five. A made-up log lists 40 of 120 students after three in one week. That shows some demand. A trial could check later demand and staff costs.
B. Sports: Buy new equipment. A made-up list has 50 club members. The writer says this proves the purchase is the best use of the grant.
C. Cooking: Try a club. In a made-up survey, 19 of 28 people said they would join. That suggests interest. The school still needs to check actual attendance, access, adult help and costs.
D. Rehearsal: Pay for an extra session. The writer says music is best, so everyone will gain.
Choose the best-supported case. Name what is still missing. This is not a final real-world budget decision.
brief.drivingQuestion: Which plan has the strongest argument? Is it also the plan you prefer?
brief.seedDirection: For each plan, list the claim, evidence and reasoning. Mark anything missing. Then rate the support.
openQuestions: Could the same evidence support a different claim?
Does a writer deal with a strong objection?
Did your own preference affect your rating?
criteria: Identify the claim, evidence and reasoning in each plan. Mark missing parts.
Rate each plan and how it deals with an objection.
Choose one plan and explain why its argument is strongest.
Say whether it is also the plan you prefer.
Use at least four glossary words correctly.
brief.deliverable: Make a table for the four plans. List each claim, evidence, reasoning and rating. Choose one, explain why, and name a limit. State your own preference.
